name: PDO thread lift

lead: A PDO thread lift uses dissolvable polydioxanone sutures, sometimes with barbs or cones, placed under the skin to reposition sagging tissue in the midface, jowls or neck without a facelift incision. The payoff people want is a sharper jawline and lifted cheeks with little downtime.

The threads are anchored to tissue and mechanically suspend it, and absorbable materials dissolve over time. A 2025 systematic review of twelve studies covering 818 patients reported improved aesthetic scores such as GAIS and FACE-Q in all cases immediately after the procedure, while noting that earlier studies had not shown long-term efficacy for absorbable threads. A study of PLLA/PLGA-containing threads found collagen stimulation in biopsies.

paras: It is done in a clinic as a short procedure with local numbing, with threads placed through fine entry points. People use it as a temporary lift or jawline enhancer and as a lower-downtime alternative to a surgical facelift. Results are described as short-lived compared with surgery.

Reviews describe mostly minor, self-limiting events such as bruising, swelling and asymmetry. A BBC investigation reported in Wikipedia found UK training courses with no mandatory qualifications and poor infection control in an undercover recording, and one physician quoted called it the most dangerous aesthetic procedure because threads cannot be removed. PDO threads are medical devices that should be placed by trained clinicians.

web.title: Thread lift (Wikipedia; resolved to the Facelift article)

angle.text: Absorbable threads suspend sagging tissue, repositioning the cheeks, jawline and neck for a lifted look with little downtime. Improvement is reported immediately after treatment; reviews note long-term data are limited.

lead: A thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure that uses sutures, often barbed or cogged, inserted under the skin to suspend ptotic (sagging) tissue. PDO (polydioxanone) threads are absorbable and are the most commonly evaluated thread in recent reviews. [1][2]

A 2025 systematic review of twelve studies covering 818 patients reported that aesthetic scores such as the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale and FACE-Q improved in all cases immediately after the procedure, while stating that previous studies had failed to show long-term efficacy for absorbable threads. [1] A 2017 review concluded that results with barbed sutures were inconclusive and that adverse events were mostly minor and short-lived. [2]

Thread lifts are marketed as a lower-downtime alternative to surgical facelifts, aimed at people who want a tighter jawline, midface or brow without incisions or general anaesthesia.[1][2] Wikipedia describes the older form of the procedure as a non-surgical face lift using barbed silicone threads to pull facial and neck skin upward without removing skin.[3] Absorbable PDO threads, which dissolve over time, are the type most commonly evaluated in recent reviews.[1] Reviews of nonsurgical jaw contouring place threads alongside fillers, neuromodulators and energy devices as options for defining the lower face.[4][5]

Thread lifting sits in a wider ladder of facial procedures, from injectables and radiofrequency through to the surgical facelift, which Wikipedia traces to Eugen Holländer in Berlin in 1901 and which has a far longer evidence base.[6][7] Public attention to thread lifts has also followed safety concerns: a 2021 BBC investigation into UK training courses is widely cited in discussion of unregulated practice.[3][6]
infobox: Absorbable threads dissolve; removal can be difficult
Physicians; training requirements vary by country [8]
Midface, jowl, jawline and brow repositioning [1][2]

paras: Thread lifts suspend facial tissue using sutures. Earlier barbed non-absorbable threads have been largely supplemented by absorbable PDO and PLLA/PCL threads.[1][2] Wikipedia describes barbed silicone and APTOS ('anti-ptosis') threads as thread-lift variants.[3]

A Korean technique paper describes a vertical vector lift for Asian patients using wedge-shaped PDO sutures, popular in Korean aesthetic clinics. [8] Other techniques include mini-midface lifts with PDO cog threads. [9]

Reviews group threads by material (PDO, poly-L-lactic acid, polycaprolactone, and older non-absorbable materials such as silicone or polypropylene), and by design: smooth monofilament threads, barbed or cogged threads that grip tissue, and cone- or wedge-shaped anchors.[2][8][10] A 2019 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology study compared Silhouette Soft and Happy Lift double-needle techniques for face and neck lifting, illustrating how product-specific the literature is.[11]

Threads are inserted through a needle or cannula beneath the skin and anchored in the tissue so that barbs or cogs grip and hold it in a new position. The mechanical lift is immediate, which is why studies record improvement on aesthetic scales straight after treatment.[1][2]

Absorbable threads dissolve over months, and researchers have examined whether a collagen response outlasts the thread. In the 2020 open-label biopsy study of 25 volunteers, PLLA/PLGA-containing absorbable suspension sutures were examined for collagen stimulation alongside nasolabial fold severity over time.[12] Practitioners and researchers differ on how much of any lasting result comes from collagen stimulation versus the original mechanical repositioning.[2][12]

Vector direction is a topic in the technique literature. A 2017 Dermatologic Surgery paper describes a vertical-vector technique for Asian patients using wedge-shaped PDO sutures, designed around skeletal anatomy that differs from the oblique, temple-directed vectors commonly used in the midface and jowl.[8]

The 2025 systematic review reported immediate improvement on several scales across twelve studies, while noting long-term data remain limited. [1] A 2018 systematic review set out to establish the current state of the art on thread-lift sutures. [13] A 2009 long-term study of 33 patients evaluated outcomes of thread lifts alone or combined with other procedures. [14]

A review of Silhouette Instalift describes most patients as finding the lift immediately effective and pleased with enhancements. [15] A 2023 brow-region thread lift paper by Sahan and colleagues was later retracted by agreement between authors and journal. [16]

A 2025 Dermatologic Surgery review of absorbable mid and lower facial thread lifts covered literature from October 2018 to December 2022 and used scores such as the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale, Wrinkle Severity Scale, Barton's grading system and FACE-Q; scores improved in all cases immediately after the procedure, the longest follow-up was two years, and complications were mild [1]. The authors concluded that in the appropriate patient thread lifts are immediately effective and the risk of dangerous complications is low, but long-term efficacy remains to be established [1]. A 2017 review concluded that outcomes from barbed sutures were inconclusive and that durability and the consequences of long-term suture presence were unclear [2].

A 2009 Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery study assessed long-term results in 33 patients who had thread lifts alone (10 patients) or combined with other rejuvenation procedures (23 patients), with additional patients who had non-thread procedures such as lipotransfer, peels and rhytidectomy for comparison [14]. A 2008 Dermatologic Surgery paper and a 2017 paper in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology reported long-term results of anchored barbed sutures and insoluble thread lifting respectively [17][18].

Human studies include a prospective single-center study of 25 volunteers, which examined biopsies and nasolabial fold severity after PLLA/PLGA-containing absorbable suspension sutures; the study reported collagen stimulation as its subject. [12] An observational study of thread lifts with Happy Lift reported outcomes in 37 procedures over 24 months. [19]

Registered trials include a comparison of PDO threads with a dermal filler for nasolabial folds and a performance and safety study of polydioxanone sutures for wrinkles and face lifting. [20][21] No registered randomized trials of long-term (multi-year) outcomes were identified.

The 2020 collagenesis study was a single-center, open-label, prospective study of 25 healthy volunteers that used biopsies and nasolabial fold severity to characterise collagen stimulation by PLLA/PLGA-containing absorbable suspension sutures [12]. A 2014 Dermatology and Therapy study of the Happy Lift Revitalizing thread performed 37 thread lifts over 24 months in patients with average aging signs needing modest lifting [19].

Thread lifts are discussed in looksmaxxing and aesthetic circles as a non-surgical way to lift the midface, sharpen the jawline or neck line and raise the brow, mainly as a bridge before or instead of surgery. Published descriptions come mainly from clinical literature and from clinics, which describe it as an in-office treatment with short recovery.[15][4]

Reviews of nonsurgical jaw contouring present threads as one tool among several, often combined with fillers, botulinum toxin or energy-based devices, and a dental review of nonsurgical modalities likewise describes combination treatment plans for facial aging.[4][5][7] The Wikipedia facelift article similarly says combining threads with other methods is reported to give better results.[6]

Wikipedia's facelift history dates the first facelift to Eugen Hollander in Berlin in 1901, with later landmarks including Tord Skoog's subfacial dissection (published 1974) and the description of the SMAS layer in 1976 [6]. Thread-based lifting arrived later as a minimally invasive alternative; a 2006 review by Villa and colleagues concluded the technique was still in its infancy but had potential, and a 2018 systematic review revisited the question after 11 years [13]. Absorbable PDO and PLLA/PCL threads have since been widely used alongside or in place of earlier barbed non-absorbable threads [1][2]. Korean aesthetic clinics popularised techniques such as vertical vector lifts with wedge-shaped PDO sutures [8].

A 2017 review found adverse events were mostly minor and self-limiting.[2] An update on absorbable thread lifts also reviewed complication reporting in twelve studies and described complications as mild.[1] Procedure-related bruising is a recognised issue in facial cosmetic work, and a 2009 study examined pulsed-dye laser for treating ecchymoses after such procedures.[22]

Wikipedia reports a BBC investigation of UK thread-lift training, noting no mandatory qualifications and describing recordings of poor infection control and punctured blood vessels. [3] An anatomical study of transverse facial artery perforators has been used in discussions of vascular safety in midfacial procedures. [23]

Wikipedia quotes the physician Vincent Wong as describing the thread lift as the most dangerous procedure an aesthetic practitioner can perform, and notes that non-absorbable threads remain in the skin and cannot be removed, so complications can be irreversible; complications from APTOS threads have been corrected with a MACS lift [3][6]. The 2021 BBC investigation found 26 cosmetic training academies in Liverpool with courses costing 150 to 5,000 pounds, and an undercover nurse filmed a thread-lift course with no infection control and several blood vessels punctured; Save Face director Ashton Collins said that people following such courses would cause complications [3][6]. In the UK, aesthetic practitioners are not required to hold mandatory qualifications, and Save Face runs a register of accredited practitioners [3][6]. A 2020 review covers anatomy, technique and the current literature on thread-lift sutures for surgeons [10].

Registered studies include a comparison of PDO threads with a dermal filler for nasolabial folds and a performance and safety study of polydioxanone sutures for wrinkles and face lifting.[20][21] Reviews repeatedly call for longer follow-up: the 2025 review's longest assessments were two years, and a 2017 review said maximum correction, durability and consequences of long-term suture presence still need clarification.[1][2]
The retraction of a 2023 brow-region thread lift paper, covering 50 patients, by agreement between authors and journal in 2024 is part of the record of this evolving literature.[16]

lore.intro: Thread lifts are discussed in aesthetic and jawline-improvement circles as a quick, incision-free lift. Claims below are the ones proponents and clinics commonly make, set beside what the published literature reports.

claims.claim: A thread lift gives an immediate lift without surgery.
Threads stimulate collagen as they dissolve.
Thread lifts can sharpen the jawline and jowls.
Combining threads with other treatments gives better results.

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs the first facelift in Berlin.[6]
The SMAS layer is described, shaping later lift techniques.[6]
Villa and colleagues publish an early review of thread-lift sutures, concluding the technique was in its infancy.[13]
Dermatologic Surgery paper reports long-term efficacy of anchored barbed sutures in the face and neck.[17]
Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery study assesses long-term thread-lift results in 33 patients.[14]
Study of Happy Lift Revitalizing threads reports 37 thread lifts over 24 months.[19]
Vertical-vector PDO technique for Asian patients described; review calls barbed-suture results inconclusive.[8][2]
Systematic review revisits the thread-lift literature 11 years after the 2006 review.[13]
Biopsy study examines collagen stimulation by PLLA/PLGA absorbable suspension sutures.[12]
BBC investigation reports on UK thread-lift training courses.[3][6]
A 2023 brow thread-lift paper is retracted.[16]
Systematic review of absorbable facial thread lifts covering 2018-2022 literature is published.[1]
